case: A 19-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 3-month history of intermittent bright red blood in his stools and loose bowel movements. His father died of colon cancer at the age of 41 years, and his paternal aunt had a colectomy at the age of 25 years. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Hemoglobin concentration is 11.6 g/dL (13.5 to 17.5). Colonoscopy shows more than 400 sessile and pedunculated polyps, most 2 to 8 mm in diameter, carpeting the colon and rectum. Biopsy specimens of several polyps show tubular adenomas with low-grade dysplasia. Diagnosis: familial adenomatous polyposis.

questions.stem: Five years after prophylactic colectomy, he develops a firm mass in the abdominal wall that is diagnosed as a desmoid tumor. Radiographs show osteomas of the mandible, and he has several epidermoid cysts on his back. Which of the following is the most likely genetic basis of his entire presentation?
options: Biallelic germline mutations in MUTYH
Heterozygous germline mutation in STK11
Heterozygous germline mutation in APC
Heterozygous germline mutation in MLH1
approach: Recognize osteomas, epidermoid cysts, and desmoid tumors with colonic polyposis as Gardner syndrome.
Recall that Gardner syndrome is a variant of familial adenomatous polyposis caused by the same gene.
Use the family history: an affected father and aunt fit autosomal dominant inheritance of one mutant allele.
questions.why: Gardner syndrome is familial adenomatous polyposis plus extracolonic growths such as osteomas, epidermoid cysts, desmoid tumors, and extra teeth. Both come from a heterozygous germline mutation in APC, a tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 5q, inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern. The extracolonic lesions mark a variant of the same disease and do not point to a different gene. Turcot syndrome is the other variant, with brain tumors such as medulloblastoma.
whyNot: MUTYH-associated polyposis also produces many adenomas, but it is autosomal recessive, so an affected father and aunt would be unexpected. The classic Gardner lesions (osteomas, epidermoid cysts, desmoid tumors) point to APC.
STK11 mutations cause Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, with hamartomatous polyps and dark macules on the lips and buccal mucosa. It does not produce hundreds of adenomas.
Correct.
MLH1 mutations cause Lynch syndrome, in which a few adenomas progress quickly to cancer, often in the right colon. Lynch syndrome does not carpet the colon with hundreds of polyps.

topics: Gardner and Turcot variants of FAP

questions.stem: One polyp in the rectum measures 3.5 cm. Microscopic examination shows long, slender, finger-like projections of dysplastic columnar epithelium over thin fibrovascular cores, making up most of the lesion. Compared with his 5-mm polyps, which of the following best describes this lesion?
options: Villous adenoma with a higher risk of invasive carcinoma
Tubular adenoma with a similar risk of invasive carcinoma
Hyperplastic polyp with no meaningful malignant risk
Hamartomatous polyp with a low risk of invasive carcinoma
approach: Identify the architecture: finger-like fronds of dysplastic epithelium define a villous adenoma.
Recall that malignant risk in adenomas rises with size, villous component, and grade of dysplasia.
Combine the two: a large villous adenoma carries more risk than a small tubular one.
questions.why: Adenomas are classified by their architecture. Tubular adenomas are mostly branching glands, villous adenomas are mostly long fronds, and tubulovillous adenomas are a mix. The risk of invasive carcinoma rises with size (especially above 2 cm), with the villous fraction, and with high-grade dysplasia. This 3.5-cm villous lesion is the polyp most likely to already contain cancer.
whyNot: Correct.
Tubular adenomas are made of branching tubular glands. A small tubular adenoma carries a lower risk than a large villous one.
Hyperplastic polyps show serrated crypts without dysplasia, are usually small and rectosigmoid, and have little malignant potential.
Hamartomatous polyps, such as juvenile and Peutz-Jeghers polyps, are disorganized normal tissue without dysplastic fronds.

questions.stem: Upper endoscopy for surveillance shows several adenomas surrounding the major duodenal papilla. A biopsy of normal-appearing mucosa next to the papilla is taken. Which of the following histologic features best identifies the segment of bowel sampled?
options: Aggregated lymphoid follicles in the submucosa
Straight crypts rich in goblet cells without villi
Tubular glands lined by parietal and chief cells
Mucous glands in the submucosa
approach: Locate the major duodenal papilla in the second part of the duodenum.
Recall the histologic marker of the duodenum: Brunner glands in the submucosa.
Match the other features to the ileum, colon, and stomach and exclude them.
questions.why: The major papilla opens into the second part of the duodenum, so the biopsy is duodenal. The duodenum is the only segment with Brunner glands, mucous glands in the submucosa that secrete alkaline mucus to protect against gastric acid. Periampullary adenomas and carcinomas are a leading cause of death in FAP after colectomy, which is why the duodenum is surveyed.
whyNot: Aggregated lymphoid follicles (Peyer patches) mark the ileum.
Straight crypts packed with goblet cells and no villi describe the colon.
Parietal and chief cells line the fundic glands of the gastric body and fundus.
Correct.

topics: Histology of the small intestine segments

questions.stem: Without colectomy, one of his adenomas would be expected to progress to carcinoma. Which of the following sequences of somatic events best describes that progression?
options: KRAS activation, then loss of both APC alleles, then TP53 loss
Second APC allele loss, then KRAS activation, then TP53 loss
MLH1 loss, then microsatellite instability, then TGFBR2 mutation
TP53 loss, then KRAS activation, then loss of the second APC allele
approach: Note that he already carries one mutant APC allele in every cell.
Recall that the adenoma to carcinoma sequence starts with APC loss, followed by KRAS activation and then TP53 loss.
Separate this from the mismatch repair pathway of Lynch syndrome.
questions.why: In familial adenomatous polyposis every colonic cell starts with one mutant APC allele, so a single somatic hit to the second allele frees beta-catenin and starts an adenoma. KRAS activation then drives growth of the adenoma, and loss of TP53 late in the sequence allows transformation to carcinoma. This is the chromosomal instability pathway. Lynch syndrome tumors follow a separate route, in which loss of mismatch repair (MLH1, MSH2) causes microsatellite instability.
whyNot: APC loss is the gatekeeper event and comes first in this pathway, before KRAS activation.
Correct.
This is the mismatch repair pathway of Lynch syndrome. Frameshift mutations build up in genes with repeat sequences such as TGFBR2.
TP53 loss is a late event in the sequence. It permits the change from a large adenoma to invasive carcinoma.

dx: Acute calculous cholecystitis from cholesterol stones
case: A 38-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of a 14-hour history of constant right upper quadrant pain that radiates to the right shoulder blade, with nausea and vomiting. She has had three shorter episodes of similar pain over the past year. Temperature is 38.4 °C (101.1 °F), pulse is 106/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 128/78 mm Hg. Deep palpation of the right upper quadrant causes inspiratory arrest. Leukocyte count is 15,800/mm3 (4,500 to 11,000). Serum total bilirubin is 1.0 mg/dL (0.1 to 1.2), and lipase is normal. Ultrasonography shows multiple gallstones, one impacted in the gallbladder neck, a gallbladder wall 6 mm thick (normal under 3), and pericholecystic fluid. Diagnosis: acute calculous cholecystitis.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains the initial injury to the gallbladder wall in this patient?
options: Primary bacterial infection ascending from the duodenal lumen
Chemical irritation by bile trapped behind the stone
Wall ischemia and bile stasis during a critical illness
Reflux of activated pancreatic enzymes into the gallbladder
approach: Note the stone impacted in the gallbladder neck, which blocks outflow into the cystic duct.
Recall that acute calculous cholecystitis begins as chemical inflammation from trapped bile.
Treat bacterial infection as a later, secondary event.
questions.why: In acute calculous cholecystitis a stone obstructs the gallbladder neck or cystic duct. Trapped bile becomes more concentrated, and phospholipase from the injured mucosa converts lecithin to lysolecithin, which, with bile acids, damages the mucosa and releases prostaglandins. The gallbladder distends, its wall becomes edematous, and inflammation spreads to the parietal peritoneum, which produces the Murphy sign. Bacteria infect the stagnant bile later in many patients.
whyNot: Bacteria can be cultured from the bile in many cases, but infection follows the obstruction and chemical injury rather than starting it.
Correct.
This describes acalculous cholecystitis, which occurs in critically ill patients after trauma, burns, major surgery, or sepsis. She has an impacted stone and no critical illness.
Pancreatic enzyme reflux does not cause cholecystitis, and her normal lipase argues against pancreatic involvement.

questions.stem: She has taken a combined estrogen-progestin oral contraceptive for 12 years. Analysis of the stones removed at cholecystectomy shows that they are composed mainly of cholesterol. Which of the following mechanisms most directly links her estrogen exposure to this type of stone?
options: Increased hemolysis with excess unconjugated bilirubin in bile
Bacterial beta-glucuronidase activity in the bile ducts
Increased conversion of cholesterol to bile acids
Increased hepatic secretion of cholesterol into bile
approach: Identify the stone type: cholesterol stones form when bile is supersaturated with cholesterol.
Recall that estrogen increases hepatic cholesterol uptake and secretion into bile.
Exclude the mechanisms that produce pigment stones.
questions.why: Cholesterol stays dissolved in bile only when enough bile acids and lecithin are present to carry it in micelles and vesicles. Estrogen increases hepatic uptake of lipoprotein cholesterol and its secretion into bile, which supersaturates the bile. Progesterone adds gallbladder hypomotility and stasis. This is why female sex, pregnancy, and estrogen therapy are risk factors, along with obesity and rapid weight loss.
whyNot: Chronic hemolysis, as in sickle cell disease or hereditary spherocytosis, causes black pigment stones made of calcium bilirubinate.
Bacterial beta-glucuronidase deconjugates bilirubin in infected ducts and forms brown pigment stones, which are common in East Asia and with liver flukes.
Converting cholesterol to bile acids lowers the cholesterol saturation of bile and protects against stones.
Correct.

questions.stem: Each of her episodes began about 30 minutes after a meal of fried food. Release of which of the following best explains why such meals precipitate her pain?
options: Cholecystokinin from duodenal I cells
Secretin from S cells of the duodenal mucosa
Gastrin from G cells of the gastric antrum
Motilin from enteroendocrine cells of the duodenum
approach: Link fat in the duodenum to the hormone that contracts the gallbladder.
Recall that cholecystokinin from I cells contracts the gallbladder and relaxes the sphincter of Oddi.
Apply it: contraction against a stone in the neck raises pressure and causes pain.
questions.why: Fatty acids and amino acids entering the duodenum stimulate I cells of the duodenum and jejunum to release cholecystokinin. CCK contracts gallbladder smooth muscle and relaxes the sphincter of Oddi to deliver bile for fat digestion. When a stone blocks the neck, contraction against the obstruction raises pressure in the gallbladder and causes pain. This is why biliary pain typically follows fatty meals.
whyNot: Correct.
Secretin responds to acid in the duodenum and stimulates bicarbonate-rich fluid from pancreatic and bile duct cells. It does not contract the gallbladder.
Gastrin stimulates gastric acid secretion and mucosal growth and has no major role in gallbladder contraction.
Motilin drives the migrating motor complex during fasting, and its release is suppressed by eating.

questions.stem: During laparoscopic cholecystectomy, the surgeon clips the artery that crosses the hepatocystic triangle to reach the gallbladder. This artery is most commonly a branch of which of the following?
options: Gastroduodenal artery
Left gastric artery
Right hepatic artery
Splenic artery
approach: Identify the artery in the hepatocystic (Calot) triangle as the cystic artery.
Recall that it usually arises from the right hepatic artery.
Trace it back: right hepatic, proper hepatic, common hepatic, celiac trunk.
questions.why: The cystic artery usually arises from the right hepatic artery within the hepatocystic triangle, which is bounded by the cystic duct, the common hepatic duct, and the inferior surface of the liver. The right hepatic artery comes from the proper hepatic artery, the continuation of the common hepatic artery, which is one of the three branches of the celiac trunk. Because the right hepatic artery often runs close to the cystic duct, surgeons identify these structures before clipping.
whyNot: The gastroduodenal artery arises from the common hepatic artery and runs behind the first part of the duodenum. It is the vessel eroded by a posterior duodenal ulcer.
The left gastric artery supplies the lesser curvature of the stomach and the distal esophagus.
Correct.
The splenic artery runs along the upper border of the pancreas to the spleen and gives short gastric and left gastro-omental branches.

case: A 67-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 1-week history of yellow skin, itching, dark urine, and pale stools. He has had episodes of right upper quadrant pain after meals for 2 years. Temperature is 37.1 °C (98.8 °F), pulse is 84/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 136/82 mm Hg. He is jaundiced. Serum studies show total bilirubin of 6.4 mg/dL (0.1 to 1.2), direct bilirubin of 5.0 mg/dL (0 to 0.3), alkaline phosphatase of 420 U/L (40 to 130), and ALT of 76 U/L (10 to 40). Ultrasonography shows a 3-cm stone impacted in the gallbladder neck, with dilated intrahepatic ducts and a dilated common hepatic duct. The common bile duct below the cystic duct junction is of normal caliber and contains no stones. Diagnosis: Mirizzi syndrome.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains this patient's jaundice?
options: Stone obstruction of the distal common bile duct
Obstruction of the cystic duct alone
Malignant stricture at the hepatic duct confluence
Extrinsic compression of the common hepatic duct
approach: Note the dilated ducts above the stone and the normal common bile duct below it.
Place the obstruction at the common hepatic duct, beside the gallbladder neck.
Recognize Mirizzi syndrome: a stone in the gallbladder neck or cystic duct presses on the common hepatic duct from outside.
questions.why: In Mirizzi syndrome a large stone lodges in the gallbladder neck or cystic duct, and the stone and surrounding inflammation press on the adjacent common hepatic duct. Bile cannot leave the liver, so conjugated bilirubin backs up into the blood and urine, and stools turn pale. The ducts above the compression dilate while the common bile duct below stays normal. Over time the stone can erode into the duct and form a cholecystobiliary fistula.
whyNot: A stone in the distal common bile duct (choledocholithiasis) would dilate the common bile duct as well, and ultrasonography shows a normal, stone-free common bile duct.
Cystic duct obstruction alone causes biliary colic or cholecystitis without jaundice, because bile from the liver still drains through the common hepatic and common bile ducts.
A tumor at the confluence of the right and left hepatic ducts would leave the common hepatic duct below it undilated. Here the common hepatic duct is dilated down to the impacted stone.
Correct.

questions.stem: Three days later, while awaiting surgery, he has shaking chills and becomes confused. Temperature is 39.6 °C (103.3 °F), pulse is 118/min, and blood pressure is 86/50 mm Hg. Which of the following best explains this change?
options: Gallstone pancreatitis
Ascending cholangitis
Gallstone ileus
Biliary colic
approach: Note fever, jaundice, and right upper quadrant disease (Charcot triad) plus hypotension and confusion (Reynolds pentad).
Recall that bacteria multiply in obstructed, stagnant bile within the duct system.
Match the stone's location in the biliary tree to its complication.
questions.why: Obstruction of the bile ducts lets enteric bacteria such as Escherichia coli, Klebsiella, and Enterococcus ascend and multiply in stagnant bile. Rising duct pressure pushes bacteria into the blood and causes sepsis. Fever, jaundice, and right upper quadrant pain form the Charcot triad, and adding hypotension and confusion forms the Reynolds pentad, which calls for urgent biliary drainage. Cholangitis requires obstruction of the duct system, which his compressed common hepatic duct provides.
whyNot: Gallstone pancreatitis needs a stone at or near the ampulla, where it blocks the pancreatic duct. It presents with epigastric pain radiating to the back and a high lipase.
Correct.
Gallstone ileus follows a cholecystoenteric fistula. A large stone passes into the bowel and obstructs it, usually near the ileocecal valve, causing vomiting and distension.
Biliary colic is transient pain from a stone briefly blocking the cystic duct, without fever or shock.

questions.stem: Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography is planned to place a stent above the compression. To cannulate the bile duct, the endoscope must be advanced into which of the following parts of the duodenum?
options: Superior part
Horizontal part
Descending part
Ascending part
approach: Recall that the common bile duct joins the main pancreatic duct at the hepatopancreatic ampulla.
Locate the ampulla's opening, the major duodenal papilla, on the posteromedial wall of the descending (second) part.
Name the duodenal parts in order: superior, descending, horizontal, ascending.
questions.why: The common bile duct passes behind the first part of the duodenum and through the head of the pancreas, then joins the main pancreatic duct at the hepatopancreatic ampulla (of Vater). The ampulla opens at the major duodenal papilla on the posteromedial wall of the descending part. The minor papilla, for the accessory pancreatic duct, lies a little above it in the same part.
whyNot: The superior part, which includes the duodenal cap, has no papilla. The common bile duct and gastroduodenal artery pass behind it.
The horizontal part crosses the inferior vena cava and aorta at about L3, passing under the superior mesenteric vessels. No ducts open into it.
Correct.
The ascending part rises to the duodenojejunal flexure, held by the suspensory muscle of the duodenum (ligament of Treitz), and has no papilla.

questions.stem: His obstruction also keeps bile acids from reaching the intestine. In health, the liver secretes several times more bile acid into the intestine each day than it synthesizes, and only a small fraction appears in stool. Which of the following best accounts for this conservation?
options: Sodium-coupled active uptake in the terminal ileum
Passive diffusion of conjugated bile acids in the duodenum
Bacterial conversion of bile acids to cholesterol in the colon
Reabsorption of bile acids from the gallbladder into blood
approach: Recognize that a small bile acid pool must be recycled several times a day.
Recall that conjugated bile acids are reclaimed by an active sodium-dependent transporter in the terminal ileum.
Follow them through portal blood back to hepatocytes for resecretion.
questions.why: About 95% of secreted bile acids are reabsorbed, mostly by the apical sodium-dependent bile acid transporter in the terminal ileum. They return in portal blood bound to albumin, and hepatocytes take them up and secrete them again, so the pool cycles several times a day. The liver synthesizes only enough new bile acid to replace the small amount lost in stool. Ileal disease or resection breaks this circuit, shrinking the pool and causing steatorrhea and a higher risk of cholesterol gallstones.
whyNot: Correct.
Conjugated bile acids are ionized at intestinal pH and cross the proximal intestine poorly. This keeps them in the lumen, where they form micelles for fat absorption.
Colonic bacteria deconjugate and dehydroxylate bile acids into secondary bile acids such as deoxycholate. They do not convert bile acids back into cholesterol.
The gallbladder stores and concentrates bile by absorbing sodium and water. It does not return bile acids to the blood.

dx: Gallbladder adenocarcinoma in a porcelain gallbladder
case: A 68-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 2-month history of yellow skin, generalized itching, a dull right upper quadrant ache, and a 7-kg (15-lb) weight loss. She was told she had gallstones 15 years ago and declined surgery. She is jaundiced, and a firm mass is palpable below the right costal margin. Serum total bilirubin is 9.1 mg/dL (0.1 to 1.2), direct bilirubin is 7.6 mg/dL (0 to 0.3), and alkaline phosphatase is 610 U/L (40 to 130). CT scan shows gallstones, a continuous rim of calcification in the gallbladder wall, and an irregular mass in the gallbladder neck that invades the adjacent liver and narrows the common hepatic duct, with dilated intrahepatic ducts. Biopsy shows adenocarcinoma. Diagnosis: gallbladder adenocarcinoma in a porcelain gallbladder.

questions.stem: Her serum calcium concentration is 9.3 mg/dL (8.5 to 10.5). Which of the following best describes the calcification in her gallbladder wall?
options: Dystrophic calcification from chronic inflammation
Metastatic calcification from a high serum calcium
Calcification within a cluster of cholesterol polyps
Calcified wall of a hepatic echinococcal cyst
approach: Note the normal serum calcium, which excludes metastatic calcification.
Link calcium deposits in damaged tissue with a normal serum calcium to dystrophic calcification.
Connect long-standing gallstones to chronic cholecystitis, and the porcelain gallbladder to cancer risk.
questions.why: Long-standing gallstones cause repeated injury and chronic cholecystitis, with fibrosis of the gallbladder wall. Calcium salts deposit in the damaged wall while serum calcium stays normal, which is dystrophic calcification. A calcified (porcelain) gallbladder marks long-standing chronic inflammation and is a classic risk factor for gallbladder adenocarcinoma.
whyNot: Correct.
Metastatic calcification occurs in normal tissue when serum calcium or phosphate is high, as in hyperparathyroidism. Her serum calcium is normal.
Cholesterol polyps are small, lipid-laden projections of the mucosa (cholesterolosis). They do not calcify the whole wall.
Echinococcal (hydatid) cysts can calcify, but they form in the liver and would not outline the gallbladder wall.

questions.stem: Which of the following sets of findings in her urine and stool is most likely?
options: Urine bilirubin absent, urine urobilinogen high, dark stools
Urine bilirubin present, urine urobilinogen high, brown stools
Urine bilirubin present, urine urobilinogen low, pale stools
Urine bilirubin absent, urine urobilinogen normal, brown stools
approach: Recognize progressive jaundice with a high direct bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase as obstructive (posthepatic) jaundice.
Conjugated bilirubin is water soluble, so it spills into urine when it backs up into blood.
With bile blocked from the gut, bacteria make little urobilinogen and stercobilin, so urine urobilinogen falls and stools turn pale.
questions.why: Gallbladder adenocarcinoma near the neck, like cholangiocarcinoma, obstructs the bile ducts and causes progressive, often painless jaundice with weight loss. Conjugated bilirubin regurgitates into the blood and, being water soluble, appears in urine and darkens it. Little bilirubin reaches the intestine, so gut bacteria produce little urobilinogen (lowering urine urobilinogen) and little stercobilin (giving pale, clay-colored stools). Cholangiocarcinoma has different risk factors, including primary sclerosing cholangitis and liver flukes such as Clonorchis sinensis.
whyNot: This pattern fits hemolysis. Unconjugated bilirubin is bound to albumin and does not enter urine, while increased bilirubin delivery to the gut raises urobilinogen.
Bilirubin in urine with increased urobilinogen fits hepatocellular disease such as hepatitis, where some bilirubin still reaches the gut. Duct obstruction lowers urobilinogen.
Correct.
This pattern fits Gilbert syndrome or another mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia. It does not fit a high direct bilirubin.

questions.stem: At surgery, the tumor has spread from the gallbladder neck along the free edge of the lesser omentum into the transverse fissure on the visceral surface of the liver. Which of the following groups of structures, passing through this fissure, is at greatest risk of encasement?
options: Right, middle, and left hepatic veins and the inferior vena cava
Portal vein, hepatic arteries, and hepatic ducts
Left gastric artery, left gastric vein, and esophageal branches
Splenic artery, splenic vein, and the tail of the pancreas
approach: Identify the transverse fissure on the visceral surface of the liver as the porta hepatis.
Recall that the portal vein, hepatic artery, and bile duct run in the free edge of the lesser omentum (hepatoduodenal ligament) to the porta.
Exclude vessels that leave the liver posteriorly near the bare area.
questions.why: The porta hepatis is the transverse fissure on the visceral surface of the liver, between the quadrate and caudate lobes. The portal vein and hepatic arteries enter the liver there, and the right and left hepatic ducts leave it and join to form the common hepatic duct. Bile then flows down the common hepatic duct, joins the cystic duct to form the common bile duct, and meets the pancreatic duct at the ampulla of Vater under the sphincter of Oddi.
whyNot: The hepatic veins drain directly into the inferior vena cava on the posterior surface of the liver near the bare area, away from the porta hepatis.
Correct.
The left gastric vessels run along the lesser curvature of the stomach toward the esophagus, away from the free edge of the lesser omentum.
The splenic vessels run along the pancreas to the splenic hilum, far from the liver.

topics: Path of bile from liver to duodenum

questions.stem: Her gallstones formed in part because bile is concentrated during storage in the gallbladder. Which of the following processes concentrates gallbladder bile?
options: Active secretion of bile acids by the gallbladder epithelium
Cholecystokinin-stimulated secretion of chloride and water
Filtration of bile water through the gallbladder serosa
Active sodium absorption with water following osmotically
approach: Recall that gallbladder epithelium absorbs sodium actively, with chloride and water following.
Note that bile acids, cholesterol, lecithin, and bilirubin stay behind and become more concentrated.
Link prolonged storage and concentration to stone formation.
questions.why: The gallbladder epithelium actively absorbs sodium, and chloride and water follow. Bile acids, cholesterol, lecithin, and bilirubin are left behind, so gallbladder bile is often about five times more concentrated than hepatic bile and can be concentrated more than tenfold. When emptying is infrequent, as in fasting, pregnancy, or rapid weight loss, concentrated bile stays longer in the gallbladder, and cholesterol and calcium bilirubinate can crystallize.
whyNot: Bile acids are made and secreted by hepatocytes. The gallbladder stores them and does not secrete them.
Cholecystokinin contracts the gallbladder to empty it. Secretion of chloride and water would dilute bile, as secretin does in the bile ducts.
Bile water is not filtered across the serosa. It leaves bile through the mucosa, following absorbed sodium.
Correct.

dx: Autoimmune atrophic gastritis with pernicious anemia
case: A 58-year-old woman with Hashimoto thyroiditis comes to the physician because of fatigue and tingling in both feet for 6 months. Vibration sense is decreased in the toes. Hemoglobin concentration is 9.2 g/dL (12 to 16), mean corpuscular volume is 114 fL (80 to 100), and a peripheral blood smear shows hypersegmented neutrophils. Serum vitamin B12 concentration is 105 pg/mL (200 to 900). Serum antibodies to intrinsic factor and to parietal cells are present. Upper endoscopy shows thin, flat mucosa with loss of rugal folds in the gastric body and fundus and a normal antrum. Biopsy specimens of the body show loss of oxyntic glands, a lymphocytic and plasma cell infiltrate, and intestinal metaplasia. Diagnosis: autoimmune atrophic gastritis with pernicious anemia.

questions.stem: Serum gastrin concentration is 850 pg/mL (under 100). Persistent elevation of this hormone places her at increased risk for tumors arising from which of the following cell types?
options: Parietal cells of the fundic glands
Chief cells of the fundic glands
Enterochromaffin-like cells
Somatostatin-secreting antral D cells
approach: Link loss of parietal cells to achlorhydria.
Without acid, antral D cells release less somatostatin, and G cells secrete gastrin unchecked.
Gastrin is trophic for enterochromaffin-like cells, which become hyperplastic and can form carcinoid tumors.
questions.why: Destruction of parietal cells removes gastric acid. Acid normally stimulates antral D cells to release somatostatin, which restrains G cells, so achlorhydria lets gastrin rise steeply. Gastrin acts on CCK2 receptors of enterochromaffin-like (ECL) cells in the body mucosa, stimulating histamine release and cell growth. Chronic stimulation causes ECL cell hyperplasia and, in some patients, multiple small gastric neuroendocrine (carcinoid) tumors. Achlorhydria also impairs iron and B12 absorption and allows bacterial overgrowth.
whyNot: Parietal cells have gastrin receptors, but they are the target of the autoimmune attack and are destroyed.
Chief cells, which secrete pepsinogen, are lost along with parietal cells when the oxyntic glands atrophy.
Correct.
Antral D cells release somatostatin in response to acid. With achlorhydria they are less active, which is one reason gastrin rises.

topics: ECL cell hyperplasia and carcinoid tumors

questions.stem: Serum methylmalonic acid concentration is 1.1 µmol/L (0.07 to 0.27), and homocysteine is 31 µmol/L (5 to 15). Reduced activity of which of the following enzymes accounts for the result that distinguishes her anemia from folate deficiency?
options: Methionine synthase
Propionyl-CoA carboxylase
Dihydrofolate reductase
Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase
approach: Note that both methylmalonic acid and homocysteine are high.
Recall that B12 is a cofactor for methionine synthase and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, while folate is needed only in the methionine synthase reaction.
Conclude that the high methylmalonic acid points to B12 deficiency through loss of mutase activity.
questions.why: Vitamin B12 is the cofactor for two enzymes. Methionine synthase uses methylcobalamin to move a methyl group from N5-methyltetrahydrofolate to homocysteine, so a lack of either B12 or folate raises homocysteine. Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase uses adenosylcobalamin to convert methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA, and only B12 deficiency raises methylmalonic acid. Abnormal fatty acid handling from this block is thought to contribute to the myelin damage behind her neuropathy.
whyNot: Methionine synthase activity falls in both B12 and folate deficiency, so a high homocysteine does not separate the two.
Propionyl-CoA carboxylase uses biotin. Its deficiency causes propionic acidemia.
Dihydrofolate reductase regenerates tetrahydrofolate and is the target of methotrexate and trimethoprim. It does not need B12.
Correct.

questions.stem: Which of the following serum markers is most likely to be decreased as a direct result of the glandular loss in her gastric body?
options: Pepsinogen I
Chromogranin A
Secretin
Cholecystokinin
approach: Identify the cells of the oxyntic glands of the body and fundus: parietal cells, chief cells, mucous neck cells, and ECL cells.
Recall that chief cells secrete pepsinogen, mainly pepsinogen I in the body and fundus.
Predict that atrophy of these glands lowers acid, intrinsic factor, and pepsinogen I, while antral G cells are spared.
questions.why: Autoimmune gastritis destroys the oxyntic glands of the body and fundus. Parietal cells make hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor, and chief cells make pepsinogen, so all three fall. Pepsinogen I comes almost entirely from chief and mucous neck cells of the body and fundus, so a low serum pepsinogen I (or a low pepsinogen I to II ratio) is a marker of body atrophy. Antral G cells survive and secrete more gastrin.
whyNot: Correct.
Chromogranin A is released by neuroendocrine cells. It rises in this disease because hypergastrinemia expands the ECL cell population.
Secretin comes from duodenal S cells, which are not affected by gastric atrophy.
Cholecystokinin comes from I cells of the duodenum and jejunum, outside the stomach.

topics: Gastric gland cell types and secretions

questions.stem: Her brother has chronic gastritis caused by Helicobacter pylori infection. Compared with her disease, his gastritis is most likely to show which of the following?
options: Body-predominant atrophy with achlorhydria
Antrum-predominant inflammation with normal acid output
Antibodies against the parietal cell H+/K+-ATPase
Hypergastrinemia with enterochromaffin-like cell hyperplasia
approach: Recall where each type starts: H. pylori in the antrum, autoimmune gastritis in the body and fundus.
Predict acid output: antral infection spares parietal cells, so acid is normal or high.
Assign autoantibodies, achlorhydria, and marked hypergastrinemia to the autoimmune type.
questions.why: H. pylori colonizes the antrum and causes chronic active gastritis with neutrophils, lymphoid follicles, and later intestinal metaplasia. Parietal cells in the body are spared early, so acid output is normal or increased, which predisposes to duodenal ulcer. H. pylori gastritis raises the risk of intestinal-type gastric adenocarcinoma and MALT lymphoma. Autoimmune gastritis targets the body and fundus, with antibodies to parietal cells and intrinsic factor, achlorhydria, and pernicious anemia.
whyNot: Body-predominant atrophy with achlorhydria is the pattern of autoimmune gastritis. Long-standing H. pylori pangastritis can reach this stage, but it is not the typical pattern.
Correct.
Antibodies to the H+/K+-ATPase of parietal cells are the hallmark of autoimmune gastritis.
Marked hypergastrinemia with ECL cell hyperplasia follows achlorhydria, which is typical of autoimmune gastritis.

case: A 27-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 4-month history of intensely itchy blisters on his elbows, knees, and buttocks, with bloating and loose stools. Examination shows grouped vesicles and excoriated papules on the extensor surfaces. Hemoglobin concentration is 10.8 g/dL (13.5 to 17.5), mean corpuscular volume is 73 fL (80 to 100), and serum ferritin is 7 ng/mL (24 to 336). Direct immunofluorescence of perilesional skin shows granular IgA deposits in the dermal papillae. Serum IgA antibodies to tissue transglutaminase are markedly increased. Biopsy specimens from the second part of the duodenum show villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes. Diagnosis: dermatitis herpetiformis with gluten-sensitive enteropathy.

questions.stem: Which of the following steps makes dietary gliadin peptides strongly immunogenic in this patient?
options: Binding of gliadin to IgE on intestinal mast cells, causing degranulation
Deamidation by tissue transglutaminase, increasing binding to HLA-DQ2
Crosslinking of T cell receptor V beta chains by gliadin as a superantigen
Activation of the lectin complement pathway by gliadin on the epithelium
approach: Recall that gliadin is rich in glutamine and proline and resists complete digestion.
Tissue transglutaminase converts glutamine residues to negatively charged glutamate (deamidation).
Deamidated peptides bind HLA-DQ2 or DQ8 tightly and activate gluten-specific CD4 T cells.
questions.why: Gliadin peptides resist digestion and cross the epithelium. In the lamina propria, tissue transglutaminase deamidates their glutamine residues to glutamate. The added negative charges let the peptides bind tightly in the groove of HLA-DQ2 or HLA-DQ8 on antigen-presenting cells, which present them to CD4 T cells. These T cells drive inflammation, largely through interferon-gamma, and help B cells make IgA antibodies to tissue transglutaminase, endomysium, and deamidated gliadin. In dermatitis herpetiformis, IgA targets epidermal transglutaminase and deposits in the dermal papillae.
whyNot: IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation describes a food allergy such as wheat allergy, a type I reaction. Celiac disease is T cell mediated.
Correct.
Superantigens such as toxic shock syndrome toxin bind outside the antigen groove and activate many T cells nonspecifically. Gliadin is processed and presented in the HLA groove.
Complement activation by gliadin is not the driving mechanism. The disease depends on antigen presentation by HLA-DQ2 or DQ8.

questions.stem: Most of the intraepithelial lymphocytes in his duodenal biopsy are CD8+ T cells. If he does not follow a gluten-free diet, chronic activation of this cell population most increases his risk of which of the following malignancies?
options: Enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma
Gastric extranodal marginal zone B-cell lymphoma
Burkitt lymphoma of the terminal ileum
Adenocarcinoma of the sigmoid colon
approach: Note that celiac disease expands intraepithelial T lymphocytes in the small bowel.
Recall that long-standing, untreated celiac disease predisposes to a T-cell lymphoma arising from these cells.
Separate it from B-cell lymphomas and carcinomas with other causes.
questions.why: In celiac disease, intraepithelial CD8+ T cells expand and are activated by IL-15 from the stressed epithelium. Persistent stimulation in untreated or refractory disease can lead to clonal expansion and enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma, usually in the jejunum. Other findings of celiac disease are villous atrophy and crypt hyperplasia, worst in the distal duodenum and proximal jejunum, iron deficiency anemia, and dermatitis herpetiformis. A strict gluten-free diet lowers the lymphoma risk.
whyNot: Correct.
Gastric MALT lymphoma is a B-cell lymphoma driven by chronic Helicobacter pylori infection.
Burkitt lymphoma is a B-cell lymphoma with a MYC translocation, linked to Epstein-Barr virus, and often found in the ileocecal region in sporadic cases. It is not linked to celiac disease.
Colonic adenocarcinoma follows the adenoma to carcinoma sequence and is not a typical complication of celiac disease. Celiac disease does raise the risk of small-bowel adenocarcinoma.

questions.stem: His biopsy is compared with a full-thickness section of normal bowel wall. The section shows tall, closely spaced circular mucosal folds covered by long villi, with no glands in the submucosa and no aggregated lymphoid follicles. From which of the following segments was this section most likely taken?
options: Duodenum
Ileum
Ascending colon
Jejunum
approach: Use the absence of submucosal glands to exclude the duodenum.
Use the absence of aggregated lymphoid follicles (Peyer patches) to exclude the ileum, and the villi to exclude the colon.
Recall that tall, closely spaced plicae circulares are most prominent in the jejunum.
questions.why: Each region of the bowel has a histologic signature. The duodenum has Brunner glands in the submucosa, the ileum has Peyer patches, and the colon has crypts full of goblet cells and no villi. The jejunum has the tallest and most numerous plicae circulares and long villi, without those other markers. Together with the distal duodenum, it is where celiac disease is most severe.
whyNot: The duodenum has Brunner glands in its submucosa, which are absent here.
The ileum has Peyer patches, aggregated lymphoid follicles in the mucosa and submucosa, which are absent here.
The colon has no villi and no plicae circulares. Its mucosa is flat, with straight crypts rich in goblet cells.
Correct.

topics: Histology of the small intestine segments

questions.stem: His serum vitamin B12 concentration is normal. Which of the following pairs of absorption sites best explains why he is deficient in iron but not in vitamin B12?
options: Iron in the jejunum; vitamin B12 in the duodenum
Iron in the terminal ileum; vitamin B12 in the proximal jejunum
Iron in the duodenum; vitamin B12 in the terminal ileum
Iron in the stomach; vitamin B12 in the proximal ileum
approach: Note that celiac disease is worst in the proximal small bowel and often spares the ileum.
Recall that iron is absorbed mainly in the duodenum and B12 in the terminal ileum.
Predict iron deficiency with preserved B12 absorption.
questions.why: Iron is absorbed mainly in the duodenum and upper jejunum through DMT1 after reduction to the ferrous form. Folate is absorbed mainly in the jejunum, and vitamin B12 bound to intrinsic factor and bile acids are absorbed in the terminal ileum. Celiac disease damages the proximal small bowel most, so iron deficiency is common, folate deficiency can follow, and B12 deficiency is less common. Ileal resection, as in Crohn disease, produces the opposite pattern, with B12 and bile acid loss.
whyNot: The jejunum is the main site of folate absorption. B12 is not absorbed in the duodenum, where it is released from haptocorrin before binding intrinsic factor.
The terminal ileum absorbs B12 and bile acids and absorbs little iron.
Correct.
The stomach releases iron and B12 from food with acid and pepsin but absorbs neither, and B12 uptake occurs in the terminal ileum.

case: A 31-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 1-year history of bloating, cramping abdominal pain, flatulence, and watery diarrhea that begin 1 to 2 hours after he drinks milk or eats ice cream. Symptoms do not occur when he avoids dairy foods. His weight is stable. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Stool is negative for occult blood and leukocytes. Serum IgA antibodies to tissue transglutaminase are absent. After an oral load of 25 g of lactose, breath hydrogen concentration rises by 45 ppm (a rise of 20 ppm or more is abnormal). Duodenal biopsy specimens show normal villi. Diagnosis: adult-type (primary) lactase deficiency.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains the rise in breath hydrogen after the lactose load?
options: Mucosal oxidation of absorbed galactose in the jejunum
Hepatic metabolism of excess absorbed glucose
Hydrolysis of lactose by gastric acid in the stomach
Colonic bacterial fermentation of undigested lactose
approach: Recognize that human cells do not produce hydrogen gas.
Undigested lactose passes to the colon, where bacteria ferment it to short-chain fatty acids, hydrogen, methane, and carbon dioxide.
Hydrogen is absorbed into blood and exhaled, so breath hydrogen rises.
questions.why: Lactase on the brush border of the small intestine splits lactose into glucose and galactose. In adult-type lactase deficiency, lactase expression declines after weaning, so lactose stays in the lumen, holds water osmotically, and reaches the colon. Colonic bacteria ferment it, producing gas (hydrogen, carbon dioxide, methane) that causes bloating and flatulence, and the hydrogen is exhaled. Normal villi separate this primary form from secondary lactase deficiency after viral enteritis or celiac disease, in which the brush border is damaged.
whyNot: Human cells oxidize galactose and glucose to carbon dioxide and water. They do not produce hydrogen gas.
Absorbed glucose is metabolized to carbon dioxide and water. Breath hydrogen comes from bacterial fermentation.
Gastric acid does not meaningfully hydrolyze lactose. Its digestion depends on brush-border lactase.
Correct.

questions.stem: He begins drinking milk pretreated with lactase enzyme and has no symptoms. Which of the following apical transporters absorbs both monosaccharides released from this lactose?
options: Sodium-glucose cotransporter 1 (SGLT1)
Facilitative fructose transporter (GLUT5)
Insulin-responsive glucose transporter (GLUT4)
Proton-coupled peptide transporter (PepT1)
approach: Identify the products of lactose hydrolysis: glucose and galactose.
Recall that both enter the enterocyte with sodium through SGLT1 on the apical membrane.
Note that they then leave across the basolateral membrane through GLUT2.
questions.why: Lactose yields glucose and galactose, and both are taken up at the brush border by SGLT1, which couples their entry to sodium moving down the gradient kept by the basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase. Fructose enters by facilitated diffusion through GLUT5. All three monosaccharides exit to the blood through GLUT2. Because SGLT1 also carries sodium and water follows, glucose plus sodium in oral rehydration solution increases water absorption even when cholera toxin is driving secretion.
whyNot: Correct.
GLUT5 carries fructose by facilitated diffusion and does not carry glucose or galactose well.
GLUT4 is the insulin-responsive transporter of skeletal muscle and adipose tissue and has no role in intestinal absorption.
PepT1 absorbs dipeptides and tripeptides with hydrogen ions and does not carry sugars.

questions.stem: Before diagnosis, a stool sample collected after a dairy meal shows sodium 32 mmol/L, potassium 28 mmol/L, and osmolality 290 mOsm/kg. Which of the following best describes his diarrhea?
options: Secretory diarrhea that persists with fasting
Inflammatory diarrhea with fecal leukocytes
Osmotic diarrhea that stops with fasting
Secretory diarrhea from raised enterocyte cAMP
approach: Calculate the stool osmotic gap: 290 minus 2 times (32 + 28) = 170 mOsm/kg.
A gap above about 125 means unmeasured solutes such as lactose hold water in the lumen. A gap below about 50 means electrolytes do, as in secretory diarrhea.
Osmotic diarrhea stops when the offending solute is no longer eaten, as with fasting.
questions.why: The stool osmotic gap estimates solutes other than sodium and potassium salts. Here it is 170 mOsm/kg, so most stool osmolality comes from unmeasured solutes, the undigested lactose and its fermentation products. Osmotic diarrhea stops with fasting because the solute is no longer delivered. Secretory diarrhea, such as cholera toxin raising cAMP and opening CFTR chloride channels, has a small gap and continues during fasting. Inflammatory diarrhea shows blood and leukocytes in stool.
whyNot: Secretory diarrhea has a small osmotic gap (under about 50) because secreted sodium and chloride account for stool osmolality, and it continues during fasting.
Inflammatory diarrhea produces blood and leukocytes in stool, and his stool is negative for both.
Correct.
Raised cAMP opening CFTR chloride channels is the mechanism of cholera toxin, which causes secretory diarrhea with a small gap.

questions.stem: Two years later, he has taken 150 mg of elemental zinc daily for 10 months to prevent colds. He now has an unsteady gait and decreased vibration and position sense in the legs. Hemoglobin concentration is 9.8 g/dL (13.5 to 17.5), and absolute neutrophil count is 900/mm3 (1,500 to 8,000). Serum vitamin B12 concentration is normal. Deficiency of which of the following minerals is most likely?
options: Iron
Copper
Selenium
Magnesium
approach: Recognize anemia, neutropenia, and a posterior column myelopathy with a normal B12.
Link this combination to copper deficiency.
Identify excess zinc as the cause: zinc induces metallothionein in enterocytes, which traps dietary copper.
questions.why: High zinc intake induces metallothionein in enterocytes. Metallothionein binds copper more tightly than zinc and holds it in the cell, and the copper is lost in stool when the enterocyte is shed. Copper is a cofactor for enzymes such as cytochrome c oxidase and for iron handling (ceruloplasmin and hephaestin oxidize iron for transport), so deficiency causes anemia, neutropenia, and a myelopathy that mimics B12 deficiency. Gastric bypass surgery and malabsorption are other causes.
whyNot: Iron deficiency causes a microcytic anemia but not neutropenia or a myelopathy.
Correct.
Selenium deficiency causes cardiomyopathy (Keshan disease) and muscle weakness, without anemia and neutropenia.
Magnesium deficiency causes muscle cramps, tetany, arrhythmias, and low calcium and potassium.

dx: Short bowel syndrome after ileal resection for Crohn disease
case: A 34-year-old woman with Crohn disease comes to the physician because of 6 to 8 loose, greasy, foul-smelling stools daily and a 9-kg (20-lb) weight loss. Over the past 3 years, repeated resections for strictures and fistulas removed most of her ileum, including the terminal ileum and ileocecal valve, leaving about 150 cm of small bowel joined to an intact colon. Hemoglobin concentration is 10.1 g/dL (12 to 16), and mean corpuscular volume is 108 fL (80 to 100). Serum vitamin B12 concentration is 120 pg/mL (200 to 900). Fecal fat excretion is 22 g/day (under 7). Two weeks ago she passed a kidney stone composed of calcium oxalate. Diagnosis: short bowel syndrome after ileal resection.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains her calcium oxalate kidney stone?
options: Unabsorbed fatty acids binding calcium in the gut lumen
Increased hepatic synthesis of oxalate from glyoxylate
Increased intestinal calcium absorption causing hypercalciuria
Uric acid supersaturation from loss of bicarbonate in stool
approach: Link fat malabsorption to excess fatty acids in the lumen.
Fatty acids bind calcium, so less calcium is available to bind dietary oxalate.
Free, soluble oxalate is absorbed in the retained colon, and urinary oxalate rises.
questions.why: Dietary calcium normally binds oxalate in the gut lumen, forming an insoluble salt that leaves in stool. With fat malabsorption, unabsorbed fatty acids bind calcium (saponification), leaving oxalate free and soluble. Unabsorbed bile acids and fatty acids also increase colonic permeability, so the colon absorbs much more oxalate. This enteric hyperoxaluria causes calcium oxalate stones and requires an intact colon. Her ileal resection also explains the steatorrhea (bile acid loss) and B12 deficiency (loss of the receptor for intrinsic factor and B12).
whyNot: Correct.
Increased hepatic oxalate production occurs in primary hyperoxaluria, an inherited enzyme defect. Her problem starts in the gut.
Calcium absorption falls with fat malabsorption, because calcium is bound by fatty acids and vitamin D is poorly absorbed.
Loss of bicarbonate and volume in diarrhea does favor uric acid stones, but her stone is calcium oxalate.

questions.stem: Her resected ileum showed transmural inflammation, fissuring ulcers, and noncaseating granulomas. Which of the following immune mechanisms best explains the granulomas?
options: IL-4 and IL-5 from Th2 cells recruiting eosinophils
Histamine release from mast cells triggered by IgE
Complement activation by immune complexes in vessel walls
Interferon-gamma from Th1 cells activating macrophages
approach: Recall that granulomas are collections of activated macrophages (epithelioid cells) and giant cells.
Macrophage activation is driven by interferon-gamma from Th1 cells, supported by IL-12 from macrophages.
Place this in Crohn disease: NOD2 variants impair handling of commensal bacteria, and Th1 and Th17 responses drive transmural inflammation.
questions.why: In Crohn disease, NOD2 variants impair intracellular sensing of bacterial peptidoglycan, so commensal bacteria that cross the epithelium are cleared poorly. Persistent antigen drives macrophages and dendritic cells to make IL-12 and IL-23, which push CD4 T cells toward Th1 and Th17 responses. Interferon-gamma from Th1 cells activates macrophages, which become epithelioid cells and form granulomas, while IL-17 recruits neutrophils. The inflammation extends through the full thickness of the wall, causing strictures and fistulas.
whyNot: A Th2 response with IL-4, IL-5, and eosinophils fits allergic disease and helminth infection and does not form these granulomas.
IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation is an immediate (type I) hypersensitivity reaction and does not form granulomas.
Immune complex deposition (type III hypersensitivity) causes vasculitis and glomerulonephritis. It does not form granulomas.
Correct.

topics: NOD2 and Th1 and Th17 responses

questions.stem: Despite adequate total calories, she develops dry, scaly dermatitis, hair thinning, and poor wound healing. The plasma triene to tetraene ratio is 0.5 (under 0.2). Lack of which of the following dietary fatty acids is the primary cause?
options: Palmitic acid
Linoleic acid
Oleic acid
Arachidonic acid
approach: Link severe fat malabsorption to essential fatty acid deficiency.
Recall that humans cannot insert double bonds beyond carbon 9, so linoleic acid (omega-6) and alpha-linolenic acid (omega-3) must come from the diet.
Read the high triene to tetraene ratio: without linoleic acid, the body makes Mead acid (a triene) instead of arachidonic acid (a tetraene).
questions.why: Linoleic and alpha-linolenic acids are the essential fatty acids because humans lack the desaturases that add double bonds beyond carbon 9. Chronic steatorrhea can cause deficiency even when calories are adequate. Without linoleic acid, arachidonic acid falls and oleic acid is converted to Mead acid, raising the triene to tetraene ratio above about 0.2. Deficiency causes scaly dermatitis, hair loss, and poor wound healing.
whyNot: Palmitic acid is the main product of fatty acid synthase and can be made from carbohydrate, so it is not essential.
Correct.
Oleic acid is made by desaturating stearic acid at carbon 9. In essential fatty acid deficiency, oleic acid is the precursor of Mead acid.
Arachidonic acid is made from linoleic acid, so it is needed in the diet only when linoleic acid is lacking. Its fall here follows the linoleic acid deficiency.

questions.stem: A semi-elemental enteral formula containing mostly dipeptides and tripeptides is chosen to improve her protein absorption. Which of the following transport mechanisms moves these peptides into her enterocytes?
options: Sodium cotransport through SGLT1
Facilitated diffusion through GLUT5
Proton cotransport through PepT1
Endocytosis by microfold (M) cells
approach: Recall that protein digestion yields free amino acids and small peptides.
Free amino acids enter mainly with sodium, while dipeptides and tripeptides enter with hydrogen ions through PepT1.
Inside the enterocyte, peptidases split them into amino acids that exit to the blood.
questions.why: Brush-border peptidases leave a mix of free amino acids and dipeptides and tripeptides. Free amino acids enter through several sodium-linked transporters, while di- and tripeptides enter through PepT1, which uses the hydrogen ion gradient kept by the apical Na+/H+ exchanger. Because peptides use a separate carrier, they are absorbed well even when single amino acid transporters are defective. In Hartnup disease, loss of a neutral amino acid transporter causes tryptophan deficiency and pellagra-like findings, yet tryptophan in peptides is still absorbed.
whyNot: SGLT1 carries glucose and galactose with sodium. It does not carry peptides.
GLUT5 carries fructose by facilitated diffusion.
Correct.
M cells over Peyer patches sample particles and microbes for the immune system and do not absorb dietary protein in meaningful amounts.

dx: Bacterial overgrowth in a blind loop after Billroth II gastrectomy
case: A 71-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 6-month history of bulky, foul-smelling, greasy stools, bloating, numbness in both feet, and a 6-kg (13-lb) weight loss. Twenty years ago he had a partial gastrectomy with Billroth II gastrojejunostomy for a bleeding peptic ulcer. Hemoglobin concentration is 10.2 g/dL (13.5 to 17.5), and mean corpuscular volume is 110 fL (80 to 100). Serum vitamin B12 concentration is 140 pg/mL (200 to 900), and serum folate is 24 ng/mL (2.7 to 17). Fecal fat excretion is 18 g/day (under 7). Culture of jejunal aspirate grows more than 100,000 colony-forming units/mL of mixed anaerobic and aerobic bacteria. Diagnosis: bacterial overgrowth in the afferent (blind) loop.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains the combination of a low serum vitamin B12 and a high serum folate concentration?
options: Autoimmune loss of intrinsic factor with a high-folate diet
Bacterial uptake of B12 and bacterial synthesis of folate
Ileal mucosal damage with preserved jejunal folate uptake
Ethanol-induced malabsorption of both B12 and folate
approach: Note the stasis in the afferent loop and the heavy bacterial growth in the aspirate.
Recall that anaerobic bacteria take up B12 in the lumen before it reaches the ileum.
Recall that many intestinal bacteria synthesize folate, which is absorbed and raises serum folate.
questions.why: Food does not pass through the afferent loop of a Billroth II, so stasis lets colonic-type bacteria multiply. These bacteria take up vitamin B12 in the lumen, so less reaches the ileum, causing B12 deficiency with macrocytic anemia and neuropathy. Many of the same bacteria make folate, which the jejunum absorbs, so serum folate is normal or high. Bacterial deconjugation of bile acids adds steatorrhea. This pattern helps separate bacterial overgrowth from other causes of malabsorption, which usually lower folate too.
whyNot: Pernicious anemia lowers B12 through loss of intrinsic factor, but it does not explain a high folate, and nothing here points to an autoimmune process.
Correct.
Ileal mucosal disease would lower B12, but it does not raise folate, and the culture points to overgrowth as the cause.
Alcohol use lowers folate, which is the opposite of what is seen here.

questions.stem: Exocrine pancreatic insufficiency is also considered. After a 25-g oral dose of D-xylose, urinary xylose excretion over 5 hours is 2.1 g (normal above 4), and fecal elastase is 380 µg/g (normal above 200). Which of the following is the best interpretation of these results?
options: Pancreatic lipase output is too low for fat digestion
Xylose absorption requires pancreatic amylase activity
The defect lies in the small-bowel lumen or mucosa
Xylose uptake requires bile acid micelles in the lumen
approach: Recall that D-xylose is absorbed directly by the small-bowel mucosa without pancreatic enzymes or bile.
A low urinary xylose therefore points to mucosal disease or bacterial consumption of xylose in the lumen.
A normal fecal elastase confirms normal pancreatic enzyme output.
questions.why: D-xylose is a pentose that needs no digestion, so its absorption tests the surface and lumen of the small bowel. In pancreatic insufficiency, xylose absorption is normal while fat is poorly digested, and fecal elastase is low. In mucosal disease such as celiac disease, or in bacterial overgrowth, urinary xylose is low. In overgrowth the bacteria consume xylose in the lumen, so the result typically improves after antibiotics. A related enzyme problem, congenital enteropeptidase deficiency, blocks activation of trypsinogen and therefore of the other pancreatic proteases.
whyNot: Low pancreatic lipase output would come with a low fecal elastase, and his elastase is normal. Pancreatic insufficiency also leaves D-xylose absorption normal.
D-xylose is a monosaccharide and needs no amylase. That is why it separates mucosal from pancreatic causes.
Correct.
D-xylose is water soluble and is absorbed without micelles. Bile acids are needed for fat absorption.

questions.stem: In normal vitamin B12 absorption, pancreatic juice mixes with gastric contents in the duodenum. Which of the following is the role of pancreatic proteases in this process?
options: Degrading haptocorrin so B12 can bind intrinsic factor
Releasing B12 from the proteins in which it is ingested
Cleaving intrinsic factor so B12 can enter ileal cells
Converting cyanocobalamin to active coenzyme forms
approach: Trace B12 in order: release from food, binding to haptocorrin, release from haptocorrin, binding to intrinsic factor, ileal uptake.
Place the pancreatic proteases at the duodenal step.
Predict that pancreatic insufficiency can impair B12 absorption by leaving B12 trapped on haptocorrin.
questions.why: Gastric acid and pepsin release B12 from food proteins, and free B12 binds haptocorrin (R binder) from saliva and the stomach. In the duodenum, pancreatic proteases degrade haptocorrin, releasing B12 to bind intrinsic factor from parietal cells. The intrinsic factor and B12 complex is taken up in the terminal ileum by the cubilin receptor. In the blood, B12 travels on transcobalamin II to the tissues.
whyNot: Correct.
Release of B12 from food proteins is done by gastric acid and pepsin, which is why low acid states can impair B12 absorption.
Intrinsic factor stays intact. The whole intrinsic factor and B12 complex binds the cubilin receptor in the terminal ileum.
Conversion to methylcobalamin and adenosylcobalamin happens inside cells after absorption.

questions.stem: His steatorrhea results in part from bacterial deconjugation of bile acids in the afferent loop. Which of the following best explains why deconjugated bile acids leave the jejunal lumen too early?
options: They bind the sodium-dependent bile acid transporter of the jejunum
They are packaged into chylomicrons with dietary lipids
They are degraded by pancreatic lipase to free cholesterol
They are less ionized and diffuse passively across the mucosa
approach: Recall that conjugation with glycine or taurine lowers the pKa of bile acids, keeping them ionized at intestinal pH.
Ionized bile acids cannot cross the mucosa passively, so they stay in the lumen to form micelles until the terminal ileum reclaims them.
Deconjugated bile acids are less ionized, so they diffuse out early and the luminal concentration falls.
questions.why: In the normal enterohepatic circulation, conjugated bile acids stay in the lumen through the jejunum, form micelles that carry fats to the mucosa, and are reabsorbed actively in the terminal ileum. Bacteria in a blind loop deconjugate them. Unconjugated bile acids have a higher pKa, so more are un-ionized, and they are absorbed passively in the proximal bowel or precipitate. The luminal bile acid concentration falls below what is needed for micelles, and fat is malabsorbed.
whyNot: The apical sodium-dependent bile acid transporter is found in the terminal ileum. The jejunum lacks it.
Chylomicrons carry triglycerides, cholesterol esters, and fat-soluble vitamins. Bile acids are not packaged into them.
Pancreatic lipase hydrolyzes triglycerides. It does not degrade bile acids, and bile acids are not turned back into cholesterol.
Correct.

case: A 45-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 1-year history of difficulty swallowing both solids and liquids, regurgitation of undigested food at night, and a 5-kg (11-lb) weight loss. Barium swallow shows a dilated esophagus that tapers smoothly to a bird-beak narrowing at the gastroesophageal junction. Esophageal manometry shows absent peristalsis in the esophageal body and a high resting pressure of the lower esophageal sphincter (LES) with incomplete relaxation on swallowing. Upper endoscopy shows retained food and no mass at the gastroesophageal junction. Diagnosis: achalasia.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains the failure of her lower esophageal sphincter to relax?
options: Loss of excitatory myenteric neurons releasing acetylcholine
Hypertrophy of LES muscle driven by excess gastrin
Smooth muscle atrophy and fibrosis of the LES
Loss of myenteric neurons releasing nitric oxide and VIP
approach: Note incomplete LES relaxation with aperistalsis on manometry.
Recall that LES relaxation during swallowing depends on inhibitory myenteric neurons that release nitric oxide and VIP.
Conclude that loss of these neurons leaves excitatory cholinergic tone unopposed.
questions.why: LES tone at rest comes from the muscle itself and from excitatory cholinergic neurons. When a person swallows, inhibitory neurons of the myenteric (Auerbach) plexus release nitric oxide and VIP, which relax the sphincter. In achalasia these inhibitory neurons are selectively lost, probably through an immune attack, so the LES stays closed and its pressure rises. In Chagas disease, Trypanosoma cruzi destroys the same plexus and causes secondary achalasia.
whyNot: Excitatory cholinergic neurons maintain LES tone and are relatively preserved. Losing them would lower LES pressure.
Gastrin can raise LES tone, but excess gastrin does not cause failed relaxation, and nothing here suggests hypergastrinemia.
Smooth muscle atrophy and fibrosis occur in systemic sclerosis, which lowers LES pressure and causes reflux.
Correct.

questions.stem: In a healthy person, manometry after a swallow shows a contraction that travels down the esophageal body in sequence. In this patient, it shows only weak contractions that occur at the same time along its length. Loss of which of the following normal mechanisms best explains this difference?
options: Slow-wave pacing generated by interstitial cells of Cajal
Relaxation below the bolus with contraction above it
Motilin-driven migrating motor complexes
Receptive relaxation of the proximal stomach
approach: Recall that peristalsis needs contraction above the bolus and relaxation below it, coordinated by the myenteric plexus.
Relaxation ahead of the bolus comes from inhibitory neurons, and longer inhibition in more distal segments sets the timing of the wave.
Without inhibitory neurons, all segments contract at once, so the bolus is not propelled.
questions.why: Peristalsis is a reflex of the myenteric plexus. Excitatory neurons (acetylcholine, substance P) contract the muscle above a bolus, while inhibitory neurons (nitric oxide, VIP) relax the muscle below it. In the smooth muscle esophagus, inhibition that lasts longer in more distal segments delays their contraction and creates a sequential wave. Losing the inhibitory neurons in achalasia removes this delay, so contractions become simultaneous or absent. Elsewhere in the gut, slow waves from interstitial cells of Cajal set contraction frequency, and motilin drives the migrating motor complex during fasting.
whyNot: Slow waves from interstitial cells of Cajal set the maximum contraction frequency in the stomach and intestine. The order of a swallow-induced esophageal wave depends on the myenteric plexus.
Correct.
Motilin drives the migrating motor complex that sweeps the stomach and small intestine between meals. It does not produce the swallow-induced esophageal wave.
Receptive relaxation is a vagal reflex that relaxes the proximal stomach as food arrives. It does not coordinate the esophageal wave.

questions.stem: She declines treatment. Fifteen years later, she has a 4-month history of worsening dysphagia, now with difficulty swallowing her own saliva, and a further 8-kg (18-lb) weight loss. Which of the following tumors is most likely?
options: Squamous cell carcinoma of the mid esophagus
Adenocarcinoma of the distal esophagus
Leiomyoma of the distal esophagus
Gastrointestinal stromal tumor of the cardia
approach: Link long-standing untreated achalasia to stasis of food in a dilated esophagus.
Chronic stasis and irritation of the squamous lining raise the risk of squamous cell carcinoma, usually in the middle of the dilated esophagus.
Separate this from adenocarcinoma, which arises from Barrett esophagus after chronic reflux.
questions.why: Food and fluid retained in the dilated esophagus cause chronic inflammation of the squamous lining. Over many years this raises the risk of squamous cell carcinoma, usually in the mid esophagus. Other risk factors for squamous cell carcinoma are alcohol, tobacco, caustic injury, and Plummer-Vinson syndrome. Adenocarcinoma arises in the distal third from Barrett esophagus, with GERD and obesity as risk factors. Both cancers present with progressive dysphagia, first to solids and then to liquids, with weight loss.
whyNot: Correct.
Distal adenocarcinoma arises from Barrett esophagus after chronic reflux. An untreated achalasia sphincter tends to block reflux.
Leiomyomas are benign, slow-growing smooth muscle tumors and are not linked to achalasia.
Gastrointestinal stromal tumors arise from interstitial cells of Cajal, most often in the stomach, and are not linked to achalasia.

topics: Esophageal squamous cell carcinoma versus adenocarcinoma

questions.stem: She later undergoes pneumatic balloon dilation, with the balloon centered on the most distal of the three normal narrowings of the esophagus. Which of the following forms this narrowing, and at what vertebral level?
options: Cricopharyngeus muscle at C6
Aortic arch and left main bronchus at T4
Right crus of the diaphragm at T10
Median arcuate ligament at T12
approach: Name the three normal narrowings from top to bottom: cricopharyngeus, aortic arch and left main bronchus, diaphragmatic hiatus.
Recall that the most distal one is where the esophagus passes through the diaphragm at T10.
Identify the right crus as the muscle whose fibers form the esophageal hiatus.
questions.why: The esophagus begins at the cricopharyngeus at about C6, descends through the superior and posterior mediastinum behind the trachea and left atrium, and passes through the esophageal hiatus at T10 to join the stomach. Fibers of the right crus of the diaphragm surround the hiatus and act as an external sphincter that adds to LES pressure. The three narrowings, at the cricopharyngeus, at the crossing of the aortic arch and left main bronchus, and at the hiatus, are common sites for swallowed objects to lodge and for caustic injury.
whyNot: The cricopharyngeus forms the upper esophageal sphincter at about C6, the most proximal narrowing.
The aortic arch and left main bronchus cross the esophagus in the thorax at about the T4 level, forming the middle narrowing.
Correct.
The median arcuate ligament forms the aortic hiatus at T12, which transmits the aorta and thoracic duct.

topics: Course and narrowings of the esophagus
